claim: Individuals of heterostylous species belong to two or three morphs with reciprocal reproductive-organ arrangement and intra-morph incompatibility.
source: Individuals of heterostylous species belong to two or three morphs with reciprocal reproductive-organ arrangement and intra-morph incompatibility (Barrett, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrett 2002

claim: Heterostyly in Primula is controlled by the S-locus supergene that likely comprises five tightly linked genes.
source: Heterostyly in Primula is controlled by the S-locus supergene that likely comprises five tightly linked genes, determining style length (the so-called G locus), anther height, pollen size and male and female intra-morph incompatibility (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Ernst, 1936; Lewis and Jones, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ernst 1936 and Lewis and Jones 1992, and by Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The S-morph haplotype carries dominant alleles at all loci, resulting in short styles due to reduced cell elongation.
source: The S-morph haplotype carries dominant alleles at all loci, resulting in short styles due to reduced cell elongation (Webster and Gilmartin, 2006) and anthers at the mouth of the flower
evidence: Supported by citation to Webster and Gilmartin 2006

claim: The L-morph haplotype carries the recessive alleles, causing long styles and low anthers.
source: the L-morph haplotype carries the recessive alleles, causing long styles and low anthers.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic model of heterostyly described in the manuscript

claim: S-morphs are heterozygous for the two haplotypes, and L-morphs homozygous recessive.
source: S-morphs are heterozygous for the two haplotypes, and L-morphs homozygous recessive
evidence: Based on established genetic model of heterostyly

claim: The absence of homozygotes for the S-morph haplotype likely results from a recessive lethal mutation on this haplotype.
source: the absence of homozygotes for the S-morph haplotype likely results from a recessive lethal mutation on this haplotype (Kurian and Richards, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurian and Richards 1997

claim: Efficient fertilization is only possible in inter-morph crosses.
source: Efficient fertilization is only possible in inter-morph crosses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of heterostyly

claim: A candidate for a causal distyly gene has been described from Fagopyrum.
source: A candidate for a causal distyly gene has been described from Fagopyrum (Yasui et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasui et al. 2012

claim: S-locus linked sequences have been identified from Primula and Turnera.
source: also, S-locus linked sequences have been identified from Primula and Turnera (Labonne and Shore, 2011; Labonne et al., 2009; Li et al., 2007, 2015; Nowak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In Primula no causal distyly gene has been isolated.
source: However, in Primula no causal distyly gene has been isolated
evidence: Statement of the state of knowledge prior to this study

claim: No plausible mechanistic explanation for style length dimorphism is available in any species.
source: no plausible mechanistic explanation for style length dimorphism is available in any species
evidence: Statement of the state of knowledge prior to this study

claim: CYP734A50 encodes a putative brassinosteroid-degrading enzyme.
source: We focussed on transcript DN148700_c0_g1, encoding CYP734A50 as a member of the cytochrome P450 CYP734A-family that degrade brassinosteroids (Ohnishi et al., 2006; Thornton et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohnishi et al. 2006 and Thornton et al. 2011

claim: No reads mapping to CYP734A50 were detected in L-morph samples of P. veris.
source: No reads mapping to CYP734A50 were detected in L-morph samples (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1

claim: RT-PCR confirmed specific expression of CYP734A50 in styles of S-morphs of P. veris and P. vulgaris.
source: RT-PCR confirmed specific expression in styles of S-morphs of P. veris and the closely related P. vulgaris (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures

claim: CYP734A50 was present in each of 154 P. veris S-morphs from a natural population.
source: Genotyping P. veris and P. vulgaris individuals indicated that the gene was present in each of 154 P. veris S-morphs from a natural population exhibiting very short linkage disequilibrium close to the S-locus (Nowak et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data and citation to Nowak et al. 2015

claim: None of the five exons of CYP734A50 could be amplified in any of 151 L-morph P. veris plants.
source: while none of the five exons could be amplified in any of 151 L-morph plants
evidence: Supported by genotyping data

claim: CYP734A50 was present in 41 S-morph P. vulgaris plants but absent in 40 L-morph plants.
source: the same was seen in 41 S- and 40 L-morph plants of P. vulgaris (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: A public genome-sequencing dataset of P. vulgaris contained essentially no reads mapping to CYP734A50 from L-morph samples.
source: A public genome-sequencing dataset of P. vulgaris contained essentially no reads mapping to CYP734A50 from L-morph samples
evidence: Supported by analysis of public genome sequencing data

claim: In S-morph P. vulgaris samples, the read coverage of CYP734A50 exons was only half as deep as for a related CYP gene.
source: in S-morph samples, the read coverage of CYP734A50 exons was only half as deep as for a related CYP gene (see below) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—source data 1

claim: The hemizygous CYP734A50 locus is only present on the S-morph haplotype in strict linkage to the dominant G allele.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the hemizygous CYP734A50 locus is only present on the S-morph haplotype in strict linkage to the dominant G allele.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of genotyping and sequencing evidence

claim: Heterostyly evolved only once in the genus Primula.
source: Heterostyly evolved only once in the genus Primula (Mast et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mast et al. 2006

claim: The same causal genes should co-segregate with morph phenotypes in all heterostylous Primula species.
source: Thus, the same causal genes should co-segregate with morph phenotypes in all heterostylous Primula species.
evidence: Logical inference from the single evolutionary origin of heterostyly in Primula

claim: The P. forbesii CYP734A50 homologue was exclusively expressed in styles of S-, but not L-morphs.
source: Again, the P. forbesii CYP734A50 homologue was exclusively expressed in styles of S-, but not L-morphs (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome sequencing data shown in figures

claim: Each of the five exons of CYP734A50 was PCR-amplified from 10 P. forbesii S-morphs, but none of 10 L-morphs.
source: Each of its five exons was PCR-amplified from 10 P. forbesii S-morphs, but none of 10 L-morphs (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Genome sequencing of pooled P. forbesii S- versus L-morphs detected no CYP734A50-specific reads in L-morphs.
source: Genome sequencing of pooled S- versus L-morphs detected no CYP734A50-specific reads in L-morphs
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing data

claim: Read coverage of CYP734A50 in P. forbesii S-morphs was only half that of a closely related gene.
source: and read coverage in S-morphs was only half that of a closely related gene (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—source data 1

claim: The presence/absence polymorphism of CYP734A50 has been maintained as a trans-specific polymorphism in strict linkage with the G locus over more than 20 million years of evolution.
source: Thus, the presence/absence polymorphism of CYP734A50 has been maintained as a trans-specific polymorphism in strict linkage with the G locus over more than 20 million years of evolution
evidence: Inferred from genotyping data across divergent species and divergence time estimates

claim: The trans-specific polymorphism of CYP734A50 indicates that it is under strong balancing selection.
source: indicating that it is under strong balancing selection, as predicted for a causal heterostyly locus (Mast and Conti, 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the maintenance of the polymorphism and supported by citation to Mast and Conti 2006

claim: CYP734A50 was present in all tested S-morphs but none of the L-morphs of heterostylous P. frondosa.
source: Indeed, in Primula sect. Aleuritia (Mast et al., 2001; Richards, 2003), CYP734A50 was present in all tested S-, but none of the L-morphs of the heterostylous P. frondosa (n = 5 each)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data and citations

claim: CYP734A50 was present in all tested S-morphs but none of the L-morphs of heterostylous P. farinosa.
source: and P. farinosa (n = 5 each)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data

claim: CYP734A50 was absent in all tested long-homostylous P. scotica plants.
source: and in none of the long-homostylous P. scotica (n = 8)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data

claim: CYP734A50 was absent in all tested long-homostylous P. halleri plants.
source: and P. halleri (n = 9) (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in figures

claim: CYP734A50 was present in all S-morphs but none of the L-morphs of heterostylous P. elatior.
source: Similarly in Primula sect. Primula, CYP734A50 was present in all S-, but none of the L-morphs of the heterostylous P. elatior (n = 15 each)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data

claim: CYP734A50 was present in all S-morphs but none of the L-morphs of heterostylous P. juliae.
source: and P. juliae (n = 2 each)
evidence: Supported by genotyping data

claim: CYP734A50 was absent in homostylous P. grandis.
source: nor in the homostylous P. grandis (n = 11) (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in figures

claim: None of the self-compatible long homostyles of P. forbesii contained the CYP734A50 locus.
source: Our P. forbesii population included self-compatible long homostyles; as expected, none of these (n = 6) contained the CYP734A50 locus (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in figures

claim: The CYP734A50 locus was present in all tested long homostyles and S-morphs, but in none of the L-morphs from two regions in southern England.
source: Unexpectedly, the CYP734A50 locus was present in all tested long homostyles and in the S-morphs, but in none of the L-morphs from both regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR indicated strongly reduced CYP734A50 expression in the long homostyles compared to S-morphs of P. vulgaris.
source: However, quantitative RT-PCR on RNA from styles of the three morphs indicated strongly reduced CYP734A50 expression in the long homostyles compared to S-morphs (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: A promoter mutation or epigenetic silencing of CYP734A50 is responsible for the long-style phenotype in naturally occurring P. vulgaris long homostyles.
source: This suggests that a promoter mutation or epigenetic silencing of CYP734A50 is responsible for the long-style phenotype, providing an alternative route to the formation of self-compatible long homostyles in nature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the presence of the gene but reduced expression in long homostyles

claim: Exon 4 of CYP734A50 was deleted in long-homostylous mutants of P. vulgaris and P. x pruhoniciana.
source: Exon 4 of CYP734A50 was deleted in both, and no full-length transcript could be detected in the P. vulgaris mutants (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by genotyping and expression data shown in figures

claim: Two VIGS-treated P. forbesii S-morph individuals showed reduced CYP734A50 expression and formed longer styles than mock-treated or virus-treated S-morphs with unaffected CYP734A50 expression.
source: Two treated S-morph individuals showed reduced CYP734A50 expression and formed longer styles than mock-treated or virus-treated S-morphs with unaffected CYP734A50 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by VIGS experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: The CYP734A50 presence/absence polymorphism strictly cosegregates with the morph type in all heterostylous species sampled across the Primula phylogeny.
source: Thus, the CYP734A50 presence/absence polymorphism strictly cosegregates with the morph type in all heterostylous species sampled across the Primula phylogeny
evidence: Inferred from genotyping data across multiple species

claim: CYP734A50 is absent or inactivated in all seven cases of derived long homostyly tested.
source: and the gene is absent or inactivated in all seven cases of derived long homostyly.
evidence: Supported by genotyping and expression data across multiple species

claim: CYP734A50 is the G locus of the Primula heterostyly supergene that determines the style-length polymorphism.
source: Together with the VIGS results, this strongly supports the conclusion that CYP734A50 is the G locus of the Primula heterostyly supergene that determines the style-length polymorphism.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of genetic, expression, and functional evidence

claim: Castasterone was present in L-morph styles of P. vulgaris.
source: While castasterone was present in L-morph styles, it was virtually undetectable in S-morph styles (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by brassinosteroid measurement data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Castasterone was virtually undetectable in S-morph styles of P. vulgaris.
source: While castasterone was present in L-morph styles, it was virtually undetectable in S-morph styles (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by brassinosteroid measurement data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Brassinolide was undetectable in styles of either morph of P. vulgaris.
source: brassinolide was undetectable in styles of either morph.
evidence: Supported by brassinosteroid measurement data

claim: Brassinolide treatment caused S-morph P. vulgaris and P. forbesii to develop significantly longer styles in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: When treating developing P. vulgaris and P. forbesii flowers with brassinolide, treated S-morphs developed significantly longer styles in a concentration-dependent manner
evidence: Supported by brassinolide treatment experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Styles of L-morph plants did not show a consistent response to brassinolide treatment.
source: by contrast, styles of L-morph plants did not show a consistent response
evidence: Supported by brassinolide treatment experimental data

claim: Corolla-tubes in either morph did not show a consistent response to brassinolide treatment.
source: as did corolla-tubes in either morph
evidence: Supported by brassinolide treatment experimental data

claim: Exogenous brassinolide treatment specifically enhances growth of S-morph styles.
source: indicating that exogenous brassinolide treatment specifically enhances growth of S-morph styles (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from differential response to brassinolide treatment between morphs and organs

claim: The effect of brassinolide treatment on S-morph style length was entirely due to increased cell elongation.
source: This effect was entirely due to increased cell elongation after brassinolide treatment (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell length measurement data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: P. veris and P. forbesii genome and transcriptome sequences identified a closely related CYP734A50 paralogue, CYP734A51, in both morphs.
source: P. veris and P. forbesii genome and transcriptome sequences identified a closely related CYP734A50 paralogue, CYP734A51, in both morphs (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by genome and transcriptome sequencing data

claim: A molecular phylogeny of angiosperm CYP734A proteins indicated that CYP734A50 arose via a gene duplication specific to the Primula lineage.
source: A molecular phylogeny of angiosperm CYP734A proteins found in sequenced genomes indicated that CYP734A50 arose via a gene duplication specific to the Primula lineage (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The four introns of P. veris CYP734A50 were exceptionally long and contained multiple transposon-derived repetitive sequences.
source: Indeed, the four introns of P. veris CYP734A50 were exceptionally long and contained multiple transposon-derived repetitive sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Comparing P. veris and P. forbesii CYP734A50 gave a Ka/Ks ratio of 0.56.
source: Comparing P. veris and P. forbesii CYP734A50 gave a Ka/Ks ratio of 0.56
evidence: Supported by molecular evolution analysis

claim: Comparing P. veris and P. forbesii CYP734A51 gave a Ka/Ks ratio of 0.31.
source: considerably higher than that of CYP734A51 at 0.31.
evidence: Supported by molecular evolution analysis

claim: The difference in Ka/Ks ratio between CYP734A50 and CYP734A51 was entirely due to a higher rate of non-synonymous substitutions for CYP734A50.
source: This difference was entirely due to a higher rate of non-synonymous substitutions for CYP734A50 (p<0.01), while the rate of synonymous substitutions was indistinguishable (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by molecular evolution analysis shown in Figure 4—source data 1

claim: Tajima's relative rate test indicated that CYP734A50 had accumulated significantly more amino-acid exchanges than CYP734A51 since their duplication.
source: Similarly, Tajima's relative rate test indicated that CYP734A50 had accumulated significantly more amino-acid exchanges than CYP734A51 since their duplication (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by Tajima's relative rate test shown in Figure 4

claim: No evidence for positive selection was found for the CYP734A50 branches based on likelihood ratio test 2.
source: No evidence for positive selection was found for the CYP734A50 branches or the branch separating the two CYP734A50 genes from their CYP734A51 paralogues based on likelihood ratio test 2 (Figure 4; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by branch-site test results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 2

claim: Relaxed constraints were supported for the PfoCYP734A50 branch by test 1.
source: By contrast, relaxed constraints were supported for the PfoCYP734A50 branch by test 1 (orange branch in Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by branch-site test results shown in Figure 4

claim: The faster rate of molecular evolution of CYP734A50 proteins is due to a reduced efficacy of purifying selection.
source: While rigorously ruling out positive selection would likely require sequences of the paralogues from more Primula species, based on the above results we favour the explanation that the faster rate of molecular evolution of CYP734A50 proteins is due to a reduced efficacy of purifying selection as predicted by theory.
evidence: Inferred from molecular evolution analyses and theoretical predictions

claim: CYP734A50 expression in S-morph styles causes brassinosteroid degradation, limiting cell expansion and style elongation.
source: Thus, our combined evidence indicates that CYP734A50 represents the G locus in the Primula heterostyly supergene, whose expression in S-morph styles causes brassinosteroid degradation, limiting cell expansion and style elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of genetic, expression, biochemical, and functional evidence

claim: CYP734A50 arose via a lineage-specific gene duplication and presumably gain of style-specific expression.
source: Evolutionarily, CYP734A50 arose via a lineage-specific gene duplication and presumably gain of style-specific expression.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and expression data

claim: Two main models have been proposed to explain the evolutionary origin of distyly.
source: Two main models have been proposed to explain the evolutionary origin of distyly.
evidence: Statement of existing theoretical models

claim: Both models postulate that the first morphological change was the reduction of style length by a dominant mutation.
source: While they differ in the sequence of events, assuming either that morphological features evolved first (Lloyd and Webb, 1992) or that intra-morph incompatibility arose first (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1979), they both postulate that the first morphological change was the reduction of style length by a dominant mutation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lloyd and Webb 1992 and Charlesworth and Charlesworth 1979

claim: The proposed duplication and gain of style-specific expression of CYP734A50 in the ancestor of the Primulaceae likely represents the dominant style-shortening mutation.
source: The proposed duplication and gain of style-specific expression of CYP734A50 in the ancestor of the Primulaceae likely represents this dominant style-shortening mutation.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic and evolutionary evidence presented

claim: CYP734A50 is a rare example of an identified causal locus in a supergene underlying an adaptive polymorphism.
source: As such, CYP734A50 is a rare example of an identified causal locus in a supergene underlying an adaptive polymorphism (Schwander et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwander et al. 2014

claim: The identification of CYP734A50 opens the way for understanding the evolutionary origin of the Primula S-locus as an iconic case of a complex supergene.
source: that opens the way for understanding the evolutionary origin of the Primula S-locus as an iconic case of a complex supergene.
evidence: Statement of the significance of the findings

claim: The divergence time between P. veris and P. forbesii is approximately 20-25 million years.
source: To test this for CYP734A50, we sequenced style transcriptomes of the distantly related P. forbesii S- and L-morphs (divergence time P. veris – P. forbesii ~20–25 Mya [de Vos et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Vos et al. 2014

claim: Classic models predict that long homostyles originate via recombination in the S locus affecting both the G and the linked female-compatibility locus, hence they are self-compatible.
source: Classic models predict that long homostyles originate via recombination in the S locus affecting both the G and the linked female-compatibility locus, hence they are self-compatible (Barrett, 1992; Lewis and Jones, 1992)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett 1992 and Lewis and Jones 1992

claim: In self-incompatible long homostyles only the G locus should be affected by mutation or recombination.
source: by contrast, in self-incompatible long homostyles only the G locus should be affected by mutation or recombination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from genetic models of heterostyly

claim: Natural P. vulgaris populations including long-homostyles occur in two regions in southern England.
source: Natural P. vulgaris populations including long-homostyles occur in two regions in southern England (Crosby, 1940, 1949) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crosby 1940 and 1949, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: When the P. veris CYP734A50 gene was overexpressed in tobacco, leaf and stem growth were not reduced as seen for other CYP734A family members.
source: When the P. veris gene was overexpressed in tobacco, leaf and stem growth were not reduced as seen for other CYP734A family members (Ohnishi et al., 2006; Thornton et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiment and citations to Ohnishi et al. 2006 and Thornton et al. 2011

claim: The lack of growth reduction when P. veris CYP734A50 is overexpressed in tobacco likely reflects the considerable sequence divergence of the P. veris CYP734A50 protein.
source: likely reflecting the considerable sequence divergence of the P. veris CYP734A50 protein (see below)
evidence: Inferred from the overexpression result and sequence divergence data

claim: The failure of P. veris CYP734A50 to function in tobacco mirrors the failure of certain mouse SRY alleles to induce correct male development in a different genetic background.
source: this mirrors the failure of certain mouse SRY alleles to induce correct male development in a different genetic background (Albrecht et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albrecht et al. 2003

claim: A causal heterostyly gene present on only one of the two homologous chromosomes in a non-recombining region should be subject to reduced efficacy of selection and stronger drift.
source: Like the male sex-determining gene SRY in mammals (O'Neill and O'Neill, 1999; Tucker and Lundrigan, 1995), a causal heterostyly gene present on only one of the two homologous chromosomes in a non-recombining region should be subject to two opposing effects. The effective population size for such a gene is approximately one fourth that of unlinked diploid genes, resulting in reduced efficacy of selection and stronger drift, including the accumulation of repetitive elements (Uyenoyama, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Neill and O'Neill 1999, Tucker and Lundrigan 1995, and Uyenoyama 2005

claim: Purifying selection should maintain the function of a causal heterostyly gene in a non-recombining region.
source: at the same time, purifying selection should maintain the function of the gene.
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions
